title: Living Under Digital Watch
text:
Smartphones, cameras and online services now collect more personal information than most people realise. Every search, purchase and location check leaves a trace that companies can store and analyse. Supporters argue that this data makes services more convenient and helps detect fraud. However, critics warn that constant monitoring can quietly erode the privacy people have come to take for granted.

Governments also rely on surveillance technology, particularly cameras with facial recognition, to improve public safety. Yet the same tools can identify citizens at protests or track their movements without any clear legal limit. Many experts therefore call for stricter rules that require transparency and independent oversight. Ultimately, the challenge is to balance security and convenience with the fundamental right to be left alone.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what do critics warn about?
options: Constant monitoring can quietly erode privacy
Smartphones are too expensive for most people

questions.text: What do many experts call for, according to the second paragraph?
options: Removing all facial recognition from phones
Stricter rules with transparency and independent oversight

questions.text: What can be inferred about people who take privacy for granted?
options: They are likely to notice monitoring easily
They may not realise how much of their data is being collected
They always read the terms of service carefully
They have already chosen to stop using online services

questions.text: What is the writer's overall attitude towards surveillance technology?
options: Indifferent, since it has no real effects
Hostile, arguing it should be banned completely
Cautious, recognising both benefits and risks

vocabulary.definition: to gradually wear away or weaken something
close observation of people, especially by authorities
the action of watching over something to make sure it is done correctly

paragraph_translations: Los teléfonos inteligentes, las cámaras y los servicios en línea recopilan hoy más información personal de la que la mayoría de la gente se imagina. Cada búsqueda, compra o consulta de ubicación deja un rastro que las empresas pueden almacenar y analizar. Los defensores sostienen que estos datos hacen los servicios más cómodos y ayudan a detectar fraudes. Sin embargo, los críticos advierten de que una vigilancia constante puede erosionar silenciosamente la privacidad que la gente ha llegado a dar por sentada.

Los gobiernos también recurren a tecnologías de vigilancia, en particular cámaras con reconocimiento facial, para mejorar la seguridad pública. Aun así, esas mismas herramientas pueden identificar a ciudadanos en manifestaciones o seguir sus movimientos sin ningún límite legal claro. Por ello, muchos expertos piden normas más estrictas que exijan transparencia y supervisión independiente. En definitiva, el desafío consiste en equilibrar la seguridad y la comodidad con el derecho fundamental a no ser molestado.
